name: count: tokens over part_tokens, rounded up
count: a full chunk is capped at max_bullets_per_chunk
why: A 1,600-token chunk would want 40 parts; the level's bullet cap still holds.

name: count: a short text still gets min_bullets_per_chunk
why: ceil(60 / 40) = 2 is under the minimum of 3.

name: count: never more parts than sentences
why: A sentence is never split, so two sentences make at most two parts.

name: count: one sentence is one part
why: The minimum never asks for more parts than there are sentences.

name: split: equal sentences split evenly
why: Contiguous parts of equal length, in order.

name: split: n over the sentence count gives one sentence per part
split: n = 1 is the whole chunk
why: One part is the old one-call-per-chunk shape.

name: split: a long first sentence is a part of its own
why: Parts close once they pass their share of the length.

name: split: a long last sentence still leaves every part non-empty
why: Parts close early when only as many sentences are left as parts still to fill.

name: split: uneven lengths
why: The first part closes at the first sentence that reaches half the length.

name: split: the 2026-09-29 megabat paragraph into 4 parts
why: The live report's paragraph: the last sentence (threats, extinctions) gets a part, so it gets a line.

name: split: a part does not start on a sentence that leans back
why: The megabat paragraph: 'They are often called fruit bats' stays with 'Megabats …' and 'Instead they rely on large eyes' stays with the sentence it answers, so no part opens on a pronoun without its name.

name: split: leaning back yields when every part must be filled
why: Three sentences, three parts: the rule never leaves a part empty.
